She rubbed the dirt from it with her sleeve, then looked toward the abandoned station at the edge of the valley.

No train had stopped there in thirty years. Its windows were boarded, its clock had lost both hands, and weeds had claimed the platform. Yet every evening, just before dark, a whistle sounded from somewhere beyond the hills. The villagers pretended not to hear it. Grandmother had never pretended.

“Some doors open only when the last light is leaving,” she had whispered on the night she died. “And some journeys can’t be taken twice.”

Mara crossed the field with the key clenched in her fist. At the station, she found a narrow green door behind the ticket counter. It had no handle, only a keyhole shaped like a fox’s head. The brass slid in without a sound.

For a moment, nothing happened. Then the whole building shivered. Dust rose from the floorboards, and the dead clock began to tick. From far away came the whistle—one long note, followed by two short ones. Mara thought of the empty chair at home, the letter in her pocket, and all the questions she had been too afraid to ask.
